title: Death by Differentiation
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes argues against differentiation by outcome, task or grouping and in favour of responsive or adaptive teaching. She accepts that every classroom is variable in prior knowledge, working memory, vocabulary, reading fluency and learning needs, but contends that responding by setting different destinations sends a message of lowered expectations, multiplies teacher workload and fools no one when groups are disguised with table names. Drawing on the Education Endowment Foundation, she describes the alternative as high-quality universal teaching with targeted adaptations where evidence shows they are needed, keeping a common ambitious curriculum and varying support instead. She outlines Alex Quigley's anticipate-notice-respond cycle and discusses scaffolding as temporary support to be deliberately removed, admitting her own failure to withdraw sentence starters. She closes by answering the SEND objection with the EEF's inclusive-teaching guidance: strong universal provision first, then adaptations based on actual barriers observed in class.
points: Hughes argues that differentiating by outcome communicates 'I expect less from you' and that students always see through disguised ability groupings.
Responsive teaching keeps the destination the same for every student and changes the support, so intellectual demand is not reduced.
She presents Quigley's anticipate, notice and respond cycle as the practical structure of adaptive teaching in the lesson.
Scaffolds must be planned for removal because a scaffold that is never taken away becomes the lesson itself, a trap she admits falling into with exam-year students.
For pupils with SEND, she follows the EEF in prioritising strong universal provision and then targeted adaptations based on actual barriers and live responses.
quotes: Let’s start with the reality. I left school 3 weeks ago and I know that every classroom is variable. Students might encounter the same task but they do not come to it as equals.
Herein lies the rub: every classroom is variable, so it seems natural to think that we need to differentiate by task, outcome or grouping. But I am here to say this is wrong-headed.
Then the worst for me is by grouping students on tables with imaginative names, like prime ministers, so they don’t know they are on the low ability table. Except, they always do.

This means placing much greater emphasis on keeping a common, ambitious curriculum and changing the support they receive. It is not about having different destinations for each student, it is about helping students reach the same destination. So, the challenge stays high and the support helps them get there.

The key is that we are aiming for independence, so at some point, the goal is for students not to need the scaffold anymore. I have definitely fallen into the trap of not taking these away early enough, when I have had year 11 students asking me for sentence starters the day before an exam.

Scaffolding is a temporary support which can help pupils to succeed before it is taken away. Some of that support might be heavy such as paragraph plans, some might be medium such as sentence starters, or some might be light such as word banks.
Essentially, responsive teaching has a simple commitment at its heart: keep the learning ambitious. Change support when the evidence demands it.
